questions.statement: Choose the meaning that the modal verb must expresses when a speaker uses it for deduction.
questions.context: A teacher explains the meaning of common English modals to the class.

options.text: Logical certainty that something is true
options.feedback: Correct. Must expresses a conclusion drawn from strong evidence, so the speaker feels certain the idea is true.

options.text: Weak possibility that may never happen
options.feedback: Incorrect. Weak possibility belongs to might or may, while must reports a firm and confident conclusion.

options.text: Prohibition of an action by a rule
options.feedback: Incorrect. Prohibition needs the negative form must not, whereas this meaning of must is affirmative.

options.text: A promise about a future action
options.feedback: Incorrect. Promises are made with will or shall, and must plays no role in promising.

questions.explanation:
Must shows that the speaker draws a firm conclusion from clear evidence, as in the common pattern must be or must have.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose what cannot expresses when a speaker uses it to rule out an idea as impossible.
questions.context: A student explains to a classmate how English modals rule things out.

options.text: Asking politely for permission to act
options.feedback: Incorrect. Requests for permission use can or could, and cannot never performs that request function.

options.text: Certainty that an idea is impossible
options.feedback: Correct. Cannot rules the idea out completely: the evidence convinces the speaker that it is impossible.

options.text: An ability someone had in the past
options.feedback: Incorrect. Past ability is expressed with could, while cannot works in the present to deny an idea.
Incorrect. Arrangements are described with going to or the present continuous, not with cannot.

questions.explanation:
Cannot is the negative twin of must in deduction: when the evidence destroys an idea, English rules it out.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the modal that expresses the weakest degree of possibility of the four listed here.
questions.context: Two classmates compare the strength of the English modals they know.

options.feedback: Incorrect. Must is the strongest of the four: it declares the idea almost certainly true.
Incorrect. Cannot is a firm negative judgement, not a weak open possibility.
Correct. Might only opens a possibility, so it sits at the bottom of the certainty scale.
Incorrect. Should deals with advice and expectation, so it does not rank on the certainty scale at all.

questions.explanation:
Might carries the least certainty of the four modals: it only opens a possibility, while must and cannot close the question.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the meaning that should adds to a statement about the near future.
questions.context: A student explains the use of should to a friend who is learning English.

options.text: An obligation imposed by a strict rule
options.feedback: Incorrect. Strict obligation is the territory of must or have to, and should is softer than both.

options.text: A guess about something completely impossible
options.feedback: Incorrect. Declaring something impossible is the work of cannot, never of should.

options.text: An ability the subject gained very recently
options.feedback: Incorrect. New ability is expressed with can or be able to, and should says nothing about skills.

options.text: A reasonable expectation about what is probable
options.feedback: Correct. Should presents the event as a sensible expectation, as in the train should arrive soon.

questions.explanation:
Should adds a reasonable expectation about the future, leaving a small margin in case the plan changes.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Luis has lived in Madrid for ten years. Choose the modal that completes his deduction: He ... know the city very well.
questions.context: Luis describes his long life in the Spanish capital.

options.feedback: Correct. Ten years of residence is strong evidence, so must states the confident deduction he must know.
Incorrect. Might not expresses doubt, but the long residence supports the opposite conclusion.
Incorrect. Should not predicts something unwise, and knowing a city well after ten years is neither.
Incorrect. Cannot would deny the idea although the evidence clearly points in favour of it.

questions.explanation:
The length of residence is the evidence, and must turns that evidence into a firm deduction about knowledge of the city.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: The lights are on and music is playing inside. Choose the modal that completes the deduction: Someone ... be at home.
questions.context: A visitor stands outside a house and reports what she can perceive.

options.feedback: Incorrect. Cannot denies the presence of anyone, yet the lights and music point the other way.
Correct. Lights and music are strong evidence of someone inside, so must reports the deduction.
Incorrect. Should talks about what is expected in the future, not about a present deduction.
Incorrect. Might not weakens the claim, but such clear evidence deserves the stronger must.

questions.explanation:
Strong present evidence raises a bare guess to a must deduction: lights and music make the presence near certain.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Rosa is only ten years old. Choose the modal that completes the ruling-out sentence: She ... be the school director.
questions.context: The school staff list is published and Rosa reads it with her classmates.

options.feedback: Incorrect. Must would assert the claim as almost certain, which her age flatly contradicts.
Incorrect. Should discusses what is sensible to expect, not what is plainly impossible.
Correct. Her age makes the idea impossible, and cannot is the modal that rules possibilities out.
Incorrect. Might keeps the possibility open, but the fact of her age closes it.

questions.explanation:
One decisive fact closes the possibility, and cannot is the modal English keeps exactly for that job.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: The train leaves at eight and it is now seven. Choose the modal that completes the plan: We ... arrive at nine.
questions.context: Two friends check the station timetable together in the morning.

options.feedback: Incorrect. Cannot denies the arrival completely, while the timetable supports it.
Incorrect. Must not treats the arrival as forbidden, which makes no sense for a planned trip.
Incorrect. Might not casts doubt on the plan although nothing threatens the journey.
Correct. A normal timetable makes the arrival the reasonable expectation, which should expresses.

questions.explanation:
A regular timetable makes the arrival a reasonable expectation, which is precisely the meaning should adds.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Pablo comes in holding a wet umbrella. Choose the modal that best completes the deduction about the past: It ... have rained.
questions.context: Pablo arrives home after a long walk through the rainy streets.

options.feedback: Correct. A wet umbrella is strong evidence of rain, and must have plus a participle reports that past conclusion.
Incorrect. Could not have rained denies the event, which the wet umbrella clearly contradicts.
Incorrect. Should have expresses advice or regret about the past, not a deduction from evidence.
Incorrect. Must not have rained negates the deduction although the evidence points to rain.

questions.explanation:
Must have followed by a past participle reports a firm conclusion about a past event, here supported by the wet umbrella.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Marina's car is still in the car park, so she did not drive here. Choose the modal that completes the open possibility: She ... have walked to the pool.
questions.context: A classmate notices Marina's car and reports what he sees at the pool.

options.feedback: Incorrect. Cannot have walked closes the idea, but nothing in the scene rules it out.
Correct. Could have presents walking as one open possibility among several, which fits the mixed evidence.
Incorrect. Must not have negates a deduction, while the scene merely leaves walking possible.
Incorrect. Should not have criticises a past action, and nobody here is being judged.

questions.explanation:
Could have keeps a past possibility open when the evidence is mixed, without asserting that walking happened.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Diego looks exhausted after exams week. Choose the modal his sister needs to give gentle advice: You ... go to bed early tonight.
questions.context: The family talks at dinner after a hard week of exams.

options.feedback: Incorrect. Must turns advice into an order from the speaker, too strong for a gentle recommendation.
Incorrect. Cannot forbids or denies an action, while the sister wants to encourage one.
Correct. Should frames rest as friendly advice, the normal choice when a family member recommends an action.
Incorrect. Might reduces the idea to a bare possibility and offers no recommendation at all.

questions.explanation:
Advice uses should because the speaker recommends an action without forcing it, unlike the order that must imposes.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Marta is sure the keys are not in the drawer. Choose the sentence that expresses her negative deduction.
questions.context: Marta searches her whole bag and every pocket of her jacket.

options.text: The keys might not be in the drawer.
options.feedback: Incorrect. Might not leaves the possibility alive, while Marta is completely sure the keys are absent.

options.text: The keys should not be in the drawer.
options.feedback: Incorrect. Should not signals that something is undesirable, not that it is impossible.

options.text: The keys must not be in the drawer.
options.feedback: Incorrect. Must not normally states a prohibition, so it does not report certainty about the keys.

options.text: The keys cannot be in the drawer.
options.feedback: Correct. In deduction the negative of must is cannot: full certainty that the idea is false.

questions.explanation:
English splits the negative of deduction: must not usually forbids an action, while cannot denies that an idea is true.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Sofia missed the bus because she left home late. Choose the option that judges her past choice correctly.
questions.context: Sofia explains to her mother why she arrived late to school.

options.feedback: Correct. Should have plus a participle expresses regret about the past: leaving earlier did not happen.
Incorrect. Must have left earlier asserts she did leave early, which contradicts the missed bus.
Incorrect. Cannot have left earlier claims leaving early was impossible, yet nothing stopped her.

options.text: She might not have left earlier.
options.feedback: Incorrect. Might not have adds weak doubt about an action, but the sentence needs a clear judgement.

questions.explanation:
Should have plus a participle is the standard shape for judging a past choice that turned out badly.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: The borrowed book carries a return stamp from 2019 and nobody has renewed it. Choose the deduction that the evidence supports.
questions.context: The librarian checks the cover of the returned book.

options.feedback: Incorrect. Might treats the overdue status as a bare possibility, much weaker than the evidence allows.
Correct. Years without renewal is strong evidence, and must states the near-certain conclusion.
Incorrect. Cannot denies what the 2019 stamp clearly supports.
Incorrect. Should describes what ought to happen, not what the stamp proves about the state now.

questions.explanation:
The modal must match the evidence: years without renewal support near certainty, so must is the honest choice.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: A sign at the swimming pool bans all diving. Choose the option that reports the rule of the sign with a modal.
questions.context: The lifeguard explains the pool rules to the new visitors.

options.feedback: Incorrect. Might not describes a mere possibility and cannot carry the force of a posted ban.
Incorrect. Should not only advises against diving, while the sign states a binding rule.
Correct. A posted rule is an external obligation, and must not is the standard modal for written bans.
Incorrect. Cannot have judges a past event, but the sign speaks about present and future behaviour.

questions.explanation:
Written rules ban actions with must not, the modal of external obligation, not with advice or mere possibility.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Carla has not answered her phone all morning. Choose the option that states one open possibility without asserting it.
questions.context: A colleague watches Carla's desk across the open office.

options.text: She must be in a meeting.
options.feedback: Incorrect. Must asserts the meeting as near certain, but not answering gives no such proof.

options.text: She cannot be in a meeting.
options.feedback: Incorrect. Cannot rejects the idea, yet a meeting is still perfectly possible.

options.text: She should be in a meeting.
options.feedback: Incorrect. Should predicts where she ought to be instead of weighing what may be true.

options.text: She might be in a meeting.
options.feedback: Correct. Might presents the meeting as one open possibility, matching the absence of evidence.

questions.explanation:
Without solid evidence the speaker keeps the claim open, and might is the modal that hedges honestly.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Elena finds the classroom empty at noon. Evaluate the four claims and choose the one that the evidence supports best.
questions.context: Elena opens the door of the classroom during the lunch break.

options.text: The students must be at lunch.
options.feedback: Correct. Noon and an empty room are strong evidence for lunch, and must reports exactly that confidence.

options.text: The students cannot be at lunch.
options.feedback: Incorrect. Cannot denies the lunch idea although the hour and the empty room support it.

options.text: The students should be at lunch.
options.feedback: Incorrect. Should only says what is expected on a normal day; the visible evidence goes further.

options.text: The students might not be at lunch.
options.feedback: Incorrect. Might not weakly doubts the claim, the opposite of what the empty room suggests.

questions.explanation:
Evaluating a claim means matching modal strength to the available evidence, and noon with an empty room reaches must.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: A neighbour heard a strange noise at three in the morning. Evaluate the four claims and choose the one whose strength the evidence does not support.
questions.context: The neighbour talks to the family about the night before.

options.text: It may have been the wind.
options.feedback: Incorrect to reject it: may keeps the claim inside the weak evidence, so the claim is sound.

options.text: It must have been a burglar.
options.feedback: Correct. Must asserts near certainty, and one unexplained noise cannot support that strength.

options.text: It could have been a cat.
options.feedback: Incorrect to reject it: could presents a cat as one possibility, which the thin evidence allows.

options.text: It might have been a passing car.
options.feedback: Incorrect to reject it: might is as weak as may, so a passing car remains a fair open possibility.

questions.explanation:
A modal must never outrun its evidence: a single night noise supports may or could, but never the certainty of must.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Ivan's friend has failed the driving test twice. Evaluate the four responses and choose the one that gives the most reasonable advice.
questions.context: Ivan and his friend talk about the driving school in their town.

options.feedback: Incorrect. Denying the failures ignores the facts the friend has just reported.

options.text: You might pass without any preparation.
options.feedback: Incorrect. Promising a pass without preparation misstates probability and offers no real help.

options.text: You should practise with an instructor before the next attempt.
options.feedback: Correct. Should plus a concrete action is measured advice that matches two failed attempts.

options.text: You must not drive ever again.
options.feedback: Incorrect. A permanent ban is a disproportionate order, far beyond what two failures justify.

questions.explanation:
Reasonable advice pairs should with a concrete next step, while bans and denials misjudge the real situation.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Miguel arrives at 10:40 and his ticket says entry was at 10:00. Evaluate the claims and choose the safest conclusion.
questions.context: Miguel reads his ticket at the museum entrance and checks his watch.

options.text: He must get in because the ticket is valid.
options.feedback: Incorrect. Must overstates certainty, because a late arrival does not force the staff to open the door.

options.text: He cannot get in under any circumstance.
options.feedback: Incorrect. Cannot closes the door completely, yet many museums still admit latecomers.

options.text: He should get in for free.
options.feedback: Incorrect. Should asserts a rule the situation does not guarantee, such as a refund.

options.text: He might still get in if the staff agree.
options.feedback: Correct. Might states the balanced judgement: entry stays possible but depends on the staff.

questions.explanation:
The safest conclusion keeps possibility alive where certainty is unavailable, and only might does that here.
---
questions.subject: ingles
